summary: Psalm 101 begins with praise to Yahweh for loving kindness and justice, then turns into a series of personal and public commitments. The speaker vows to pursue a blameless life, reject evil and deceit, favor the faithful, and remove wickedness from Yahweh’s city.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows a royal or governing voice measuring leadership by worship, household integrity, public justice, and truthful company. In Book IV of Psalms, it places human rule under Yahweh’s standards rather than treating power as self-justifying.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David.” In Psalms, Davidic headings are ancient features of the collection, but readers differ on whether they mark authorship, association, dedication, or collection identity in every case.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the psalm as Scripture.
context.date: Psalms is an anthology formed over time; this chapter should not be assigned a precise date from this chapter alone.
context.setting: The poem speaks from the perspective of someone responsible for a house, servants, the land, and Yahweh’s city, but it does not narrate a specific event.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic prayer or vow, using repeated “I will” statements to describe praise, integrity, rejection of evil, and public judgment.

outline.heading: Praise for loving kindness and justice
outline.note: The psalm opens by addressing Yahweh and naming loving kindness and justice as the song’s subject.

outline.heading: A blameless life at home
outline.note: The speaker vows careful conduct and a blameless heart within the house, while asking when Yahweh will come to him.

outline.heading: Rejecting vile and perverse ways
outline.note: The speaker refuses vile things, faithless deeds, a perverse heart, and evil.

outline.heading: Refusing slander and pride
outline.note: The speaker says secret slander and arrogance will not be tolerated.

outline.heading: Choosing the faithful and excluding deceit
outline.note: The faithful of the land are welcomed as companions and servants, while deceit and falsehood are barred from the house.

outline.heading: Judgment in Yahweh’s city
outline.note: The psalm ends with a vow to keep removing the wicked and workers of iniquity from Yahweh’s city.

keyVerses.text: A Psalm by David. I will sing of loving kindness and justice. To you, Yahweh, I will sing praises.
keyVerses.why: This opening sets the psalm’s two central concerns together: worship directed to Yahweh and a public commitment to justice.

keyVerses.text: I will be careful to live a blameless life. When will you come to me? I will walk within my house with a blameless heart.
keyVerses.why: The verse anchors the psalm’s focus on integrity that begins inside the speaker’s own house, not only in public action.

keyVerses.text: My eyes will be on the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me. He who walks in a perfect way, he will serve me.
keyVerses.why: This verse shows the positive side of the psalm’s commitments: the speaker is not only rejecting evil but seeking faithful companions and servants.

keyVerses.text: Morning by morning, I will destroy all the wicked of the land, to cut off all the workers of iniquity from Yahweh’s city.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse gives the psalm its strongest public and judicial language, moving from household integrity to the protection of Yahweh’s city.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading says it is “by David,” and the voice speaks like someone with authority over a house, servants, the land, and Yahweh’s city. Readers differ on how much the Davidic heading establishes: some read it as Davidic authorship, while others see it as association with David, a Davidic collection, or a royal style. The chapter itself presents a governing voice making vows before Yahweh.

questions.question: What are “loving kindness and justice” doing together at the start?
questions.answer: The psalm begins by singing both qualities to Yahweh before describing the speaker’s own conduct. In the chapter, praise and public ethics belong together: the speaker worships Yahweh and then vows to act against deceit, slander, arrogance, and wickedness. The verse does not explain the full meaning of either term, but it frames the rest of the psalm.

questions.question: What does “blameless” mean here?
questions.answer: The psalm uses “blameless” for the speaker’s intended way of life and heart within the house. It describes integrity or wholeness of conduct in this chapter, not a claim that the speaker has never failed. The same verse holds the vow together with a question to Yahweh: “When will you come to me?”

questions.question: Why does the psalm mention the speaker’s house?
questions.answer: The house is the first place where the speaker’s commitments must be visible. Verse 2 speaks of a blameless heart within the house, and verse 7 says that deceit and falsehood will not be allowed to dwell or be established there. The poem treats private surroundings and public leadership as connected.

questions.question: Is the speaker rejecting people or rejecting their actions?
questions.answer: The psalm names both actions and people associated with them. It rejects vile things, faithless deeds, evil, slander, arrogance, deceit, falsehood, wickedness, and workers of iniquity. The chapter’s language is sharply selective about who may remain near the speaker, especially in the house and in Yahweh’s city.

questions.question: Why is secret slander singled out?
questions.answer: Verse 5 focuses on harm done “secretly” against a neighbor. In this psalm, truthful and trustworthy speech is a requirement for being near the speaker, since verse 7 also bars the one who speaks falsehood. The chapter presents hidden verbal harm as a public danger, not a minor private flaw.

questions.question: What kind of people does the speaker want near him?
questions.answer: Verse 6 names “the faithful of the land” and the one who “walks in a perfect way.” These are the people the speaker wants to dwell with him and serve him. The positive standard stands beside the negative exclusions in verses 3-5 and 7-8.

questions.question: How should a first-time reader handle the harsh line about destroying the wicked?
questions.answer: Verse 8 uses strong royal or judicial language: “Morning by morning” the speaker will remove the wicked and workers of iniquity from Yahweh’s city. The chapter depicts an ancient governing voice pledging decisive public judgment; it should not be lifted directly into private revenge or modern policy without recognizing that historical distance. Readers may differ over whether the verse is best heard as an ideal royal vow, a liturgical prayer for righteous rule, or both.

questions.question: What is “Yahweh’s city”?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in the final verse as the place from which the speaker wants workers of iniquity cut off. The psalm does not name the city in this chapter, though Psalms often orient worship and rule toward Jerusalem. The important point within this chapter is that the city belongs to Yahweh, so public order is measured before God.

glossary.def: A quality named in the opening line as one of the things the speaker sings about to Yahweh.
A central concern in verse 1 that frames the speaker’s later vows about truthful conduct and judgment.
The word used for the life and heart the speaker intends to maintain, especially within the house.
The people of the land whom the speaker wants near him, in contrast to those who practice deceit or speak falsehood.
The wrongdoing associated with the workers whom the speaker says he will cut off from Yahweh’s city.
